questions.question_text:
Find
∫ [sqrt(x)(2x - 5)] / 3 dx
writing each term in simplest form. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Attempts to multiply out the brackets of the numerator sqrt(x)(2x-5) and writes the expression as a sum of terms with fractional indices, e.g. (2/3)x^(3/2) - (5/3)x^(1/2). Award for achieving at least one correct index of x^(3/2) or x^(1/2) from a correct method (the divisor of 3 does not need to be considered for this mark). A1: (2/3)x^(3/2) - (5/3)x^(1/2), or equivalent unsimplified form such as (2x^(3/2)-5x^(1/2))/3 (may be implied by further work; coefficients must be exact). dM1: Increases the power by 1 on an x^n term with a fractional index (the index does not need to be processed), e.g. ...x^(3/2+1) or ...x^(1/2+1); dependent on the previous method mark, so at least one term must have had a correct index. A1: (4/15)x^(5/2) - (10/9)x^(3/2) + c, or an exact simplified equivalent with fractions in lowest terms and indices processed. (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.

f(x) = 4x^3 + 5x^2 - 10x + 4a, x ∈ ℝ, where a is a positive constant.

Given (x - a) is a factor of f(x),
(a) show that
a(4a^2 + 5a - 6) = 0 (2)
(b) Hence
 (i) find the value of a
 (ii) use algebra to find the exact solutions of the equation
f(x) = 3 (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts f(a) = 0, leading to an equation in a only, and attempts to take a factor of a out (condone slips; the "=0" may appear on a later line, but must be seen at some point in the solution). A1*: Achieves a(4a^2+5a-6) = 0 with no errors, including brackets (minimum acceptable is 4a^3+5a^2-10a+4a=0 => a(4a^2+5a-6)=0; given answer, so working must be fully shown, and simply finding a and substituting it into f(x) does not score). (2 marks)
(b)(i) B1: Deduces that a = 3/4 only (may be implied by their resultant cubic); if (b)(ii) is repeated using other roots for which a ≠ 3/4, those solutions must be rejected. (ii) M1: Attempts to substitute a = 3/4 (which must be positive) into f(x), sets f(x) = 3 and collects terms on one side (=0 may be implied); condone arithmetical/sign slips. B1: x = 0 is a solution (this mark cannot be scored if they proceed directly to the roots without taking a factor of x out first). A1: x = (-5 ± sqrt(185))/8 (and these values only), or exact equivalent; withhold if the fraction line was clearly not intended to cover both terms. (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
Relative to a fixed origin O,
• the point A has position vector 5i + 3j + 2k
• the point B has position vector 2i + 4j + ak
where a is a positive integer.
(a) Show that |OA| = sqrt(38) (1)
(b) Find the smallest value of a for which
|OB| > |OA| (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1*: Shows the magnitude of OA is sqrt(38); must see 5^2+3^2+2^2 (or 25+9+4) explicitly forming the value 38 or sqrt(38) - we need to see how sqrt(38) is formed from the three components (do not penalise poor vector/magnitude notation as long as the intention is clear; may find |AO| instead, which is acceptable). Withhold this mark for incorrect working such as |OA| = 5^2+3^2+2^2 = 38 => |OA| = sqrt(38) (the equals signs must be consistent). (1 mark)
(b) M1: Attempts to find |OB|^2 (or |OB|) in terms of a and substitutes a positive integer for a to find a value, e.g. |OB|^2 = 20+a^2 => when a=2, 24; or sets up an equation/inequality e.g. 20+a^2 > 38 and proceeds to a^2 > ... (condone sign slips in the rearrangement only; allow use of =, < or > for this mark). A1: a = 5 cso (answer on its own with no incorrect working scores M1A1); withhold this mark if |OB|^2 (or |OB|) is incorrect, or if at any point they set |OB| < |OA|, but accept an argument leading to a=5 from either |OB| > |OA| or |OB| = |OA|. (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.

The curve C has equation y = f(x) where x ∈ ℝ
Given that
• f'(x) = 2x + (1/2)cos x
• the curve has a stationary point with x coordinate α
• α is small
(a) use the small angle approximation for cos x to estimate the value of α to 3 decimal places. (3)

The point P(0, 3) lies on C
(b) Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at P, giving your answer in the form y = mx + c, where m and c are constants to be found. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Fully substitutes cos x = 1 - x^2/2 into the derivative and sets equal to 0, e.g. 2α + (1/2)(1 - α^2/2) = 0 (accept in terms of x or another variable). dM1: Attempts to multiply out to achieve a three-term quadratic (=0) and attempts to find a value for α (allow solving via any method; condone slips); dependent on the previous method mark. A1: α = -0.243 (3dp) only cao - can only be scored if a correct 3TQ is seen, and if both roots are found the other must be rejected (a bare decimal answer with no working scores 0). (3 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to find the gradient of the curve at x=0 (x=0 must be fully substituted and a value found for the gradient) and achieves an equation of the form y = "f'(0)"x + 3 (also allow via the small angle approximation for f'(x); do not allow use of the gradient of the normal). A1: y = (1/2)x + 3, or equivalent in the form y=mx+c (stating just m=0.5, c=3 without the correct equation is A0); isw. (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
A continuous curve has equation y = f(x). The table shows corresponding values of x and y for this curve, where a and b are constants.

x: 3, 3.2, 3.4, 3.6, 3.8, 4
y: a, 16.8, b, 20.2, 18.7, 13.5

The trapezium rule is used, with all the y values in the table, to find an approximate area under the curve between x = 3 and x = 4
Given that this area is 17.59
(a) show that a + 2b = 51 (3)

Given also that the sum of all the y values in the table is 97.2
(b) find the value of a and the value of b (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: States or uses h = 0.2 oe. M1: Forms the equation (1/2)*"0.2"*{a+13.5+2(16.8+b+20.2+18.7)} = 17.59 oe (condone copying slips; as a minimum accept e.g. "0.1"*{a+13.5+2(55.7+b)} = 17.59; condone invisible brackets as long as recovered/implied later; also allow a complete method summing the areas of the individual trapezia). A1*: A rigorous argument leading to a+2b=51 with no errors, including correctly dealing with both sets of brackets, e.g. ...=>a+13.5+2b+111.4=175.9=>a+2b=51 is fine, but a+2b≈51 as the final answer is A0 (given answer, so working must be fully shown). (3 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to form the equation a+16.8+b+20.2+18.7+13.5=97.2 (condoning copying errors, may just be stated as a+b=28) and attempts to solve simultaneously with the given (or their part (a)) equation; do not be too concerned with the process, as calculators may be used - score if values for a or b are reached. A1: a=5 or b=23. A1: a=5 and b=23 (both values correct). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
Given that
a = log2 x
b = log2(x + 8)
Express in terms of a and/or b
(a) log2 sqrt(x) (1)
(b) log2(x^2 + 8x) (2)
(c) log2(8 + 64/x)
 Give your answer in simplest form. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
Condone omission of base 2 throughout.
(a) B1: a/2, or 0.5a, isw. (1 mark)
(b) M1: Takes a factor of x out of the bracket to achieve log2[x(x+8)] and attempts to apply the addition law of logs, usually leading to log2 x + log2(x+8) (condone missing brackets or omission of base 2; may be implied by a correct answer; allow if they write log2 x + log2 x + log2 8, an answer of 2a+3 scores M1A0). A1: a+b, or simplified equivalent (isw). (2 marks)
(c) B1: Writes 8 + 64/x as a single fraction, e.g. (8x+64)/x or 8(x+8)/x or 8x^(-1)(x+8) (may be implied by later work e.g. log2 8 - log2 x + log2(x+8)). M1: Attempts to apply the laws of logs, uses log2 8 = 3 and proceeds to 3 ± log2 x ± log2(x+8) (may be implied by 3±b±a; condone invisible brackets around x+8 and omission of base 2; note log2(x+8) written as log2 x + log2 8 is M0). A1: 3+b-a, or simplified equivalent (isw). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
The function f is defined by
f(x) = 3 + sqrt(x - 2), x ∈ ℝ, x > 2
(a) State the range of f (1)
(b) Find f^(-1) (3)

The function g is defined by
g(x) = 15/(x - 3), x ∈ ℝ, x ≠ 3
(c) Find gf(6) (2)
(d) Find the exact value of the constant a for which
f(a^2 + 2) = g(a) (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: f(x) > 3 oe, e.g. y>3, range>3, f(x)∈(3,∞), {f(x):f(x)>3}, f>3, but not e.g. x>3, f(x)≥3, [3,∞). (1 mark)
(b) M1: Sets y = 3+sqrt(x-2) and attempts to make x the subject (or vice versa), with the correct order of operations, scoring for an expression of the form x = (y±3)^2±2 or y = (x±3)^2±2. A1: f^(-1)(x) = (x-3)^2+2, also accept f^(-1): x -> (x-3)^2+2, or equivalent expressions such as f^(-1)(x)=x^2-6x+11 (simplified or unsimplified). B1ft: x > 3, following through on their part (a) (omission of x∈ℝ condoned; also accept x∈("3",∞) or {x:x>"3"}). (3 marks)
(c) M1: Substitutes x=6 into f and substitutes the result into g to find a value for gf(6) (condone arithmetical/bracket slips, but must proceed to a value): f(6)=3+sqrt(6-2)=5 => g("5")=15/("5"-3). A1: 15/2 only oe, isw once a correct answer is seen. (2 marks)
(d) M1: Attempts to form the equation 3+sqrt(a^2+2-2) = 15/(a-3), and proceeds to a quadratic in a (usually a^2=k or a^2-k=15; condone arithmetical, miscopying and sign slips, and condone equations which would lead to complex roots; may be implied by a correct exact answer). A1: a = 2*sqrt(6) or accept sqrt(24) (must reject the negative solution a=-2*sqrt(6) since f(a^2+2)≠g(a) when a=-2*sqrt(6)); isw, but a decimal answer alone, or multiple answers e.g. ±sqrt(24), score A0. (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 1 shows the plan view of a stage (diagram not accurately drawn). The plan view shows two congruent triangles ABO and GFO joined to a sector OCDEO of a circle, centre O, where
• angle COE = 2.3 radians
• arc length CDE = 27.6 m
• AOG is a straight line of length 15 m
The front of the stage runs from B to C to D to E to F (the arc CDE joining C to E, with B and F the outer vertices of the two triangles), and the back of the stage is the straight line AOG, with O the centre of the sector.

(a) Show that OC = 12 m. (2)
(b) Show that the size of angle AOB is 0.421 radians correct to 3 decimal places. (2)

Given that the total length of the front of the stage, BCDEF, is 35 m,
(c) find the total area of the stage, giving your answer to the nearest square metre. (6)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Uses arc length l=rθ with l=27.6 and θ=2.3 correctly substituted (may use a different letter for OC, e.g. r; values just need to be embedded in an equation, or an expression for OC such as 27.6/2.3; working in degrees is acceptable). A1*: Achieves OC=12(m) with no errors seen, e.g. OC=27.6/2.3=12(m); must show at least this calculation - simply stating 27.6/2.3=12(m) on its own without linking to OC is M1A0* (given answer, so working must be fully shown). (2 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to subtract 2.3 from π (which may be implied by an expression for angle AOB that is not the given answer), e.g. (π-2.3) or π/2 - 1.15; may work in degrees, e.g. 180 - awrt132. A1*: Achieves 0.421 (rad) with no errors seen, e.g. angle AOB = (π-2.3)/2 = 0.421 (rad); if working in degrees, must show the conversion back to radians (given answer, so working must be fully shown). (2 marks)
(c) M1: Attempts to use sector area A=(1/2)r^2θ with r=12 and θ=2.3 (values embedded in the formula is sufficient; may be implied by a correct answer or further work). A1: awrt 166 (m^2) for the sector area (may be implied by later work). B1: A correct expression or value for the length OB (or OF), e.g. OB = (35-27.6)/2 + 12 = 15.7 (may be implied by a correct value for the area of a congruent triangle). M1: Attempts to find the area of at least one of the two congruent triangles using their OB=15.7, OA=7.5 and angle AOB=0.421 in (1/2)*OA*OB*sin(angle AOB) (may work in degrees; omitting the sine would give a value close to the triangle's area but scores M0). dM1: Solves the problem by combining appropriate areas together (usually the sum of the areas of the two congruent triangles and the area of the sector) to give the total area of the stage; dependent on the previous method marks and the B mark. A1: awrt 214 (m^2) (condone lack of units; must follow from a correct method, isw if they round incorrectly). (6 marks)

questions.question_text:
The first three terms of a geometric sequence are
3k + 4, 12 - 3k, k + 16
where k is a constant.
(a) Show that k satisfies the equation
3k^2 - 62k + 40 = 0 (2)

Given that the sequence converges,
(b) (i) find the value of k, giving a reason for your answer,
 (ii) find the value of S∞ (5)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Forms a correct equation linking the three terms using the common-ratio property of a geometric sequence, e.g. (12-3k)/(3k+4) = (k+16)/(12-3k) (condone invisible brackets if implied by further work; other equivalent set-ups using the nth term or sum formulae are also acceptable). A1*: Achieves the given quadratic 3k^2-62k+40=0 with no errors, including invisible brackets; cannot be scored by proceeding in a single step from the starting equation - must involve multiplying out brackets or dealing with fractions (given answer, so working must be fully shown). (2 marks)
(b)(i) M1: Attempts to solve the given quadratic, achieving at least one value for k (usual rules for solving a quadratic apply; may be achieved directly from a calculator). A1: k=20, with correct reasoning (if r is found anywhere in part (i) it must be correct), e.g. "k=20 since r=-3/4 which is between -1 and 1", or by listing at least two consecutive terms for k=20 (must be correct, e.g. 64, -48) with a comment that the numbers are getting smaller in magnitude; a bare statement that the sequence "is converging" is not sufficient, and k=2/3 (giving r=5/3>1) must be rejected with a reason. (ii) B1: a=64 and r=-3/4 oe (or allow a=6 and r=5/3 oe); may be implied by later work or a correct calculation using these values. M1: A full attempt to find S∞ by using their value of k to reach a value for r with |r|<1 and a value for a, and substituting correctly into a/(1-r) (condone sign slips in calculating a and r only; they cannot just substitute their k as r, and manually summing many terms does not score this mark). A1: S∞ = 256/7 cao (do not allow 36.6, as this is not S∞); isw after a correct exact answer is seen. (5 marks)

questions.question_text:
A circle C has equation
x^2 + y^2 + 6kx - 2ky + 7 = 0
where k is a constant.
(a) Find in terms of k,
 (i) the coordinates of the centre of C
 (ii) the radius of C (3)

The line with equation y = 2x - 1 intersects C at 2 distinct points.
(b) Find the range of possible values of k. (6)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a)(i) B1: Centre (-3k, k) oe, accept without brackets, may be written as x=-3k, y=k. (ii) M1: Attempts to find r^2 by completing the square and collecting terms outside the brackets on the other side of the equation, e.g. (x±3k)^2 - ...k^2 + (y±k)^2 - ...k^2 + 7 = 0 => (x±3k)^2+(y±k)^2 = ±ak^2±b (alternatively uses the general formula r^2 = f^2+g^2-c; may also be implied by an expression for r). A1ft: radius = sqrt(10k^2-7) (condone unsimplified equivalents such as sqrt(9k^2+k^2-7); do not allow if left embedded in the equation of the circle rather than explicitly extracted; only follow through on a centre of the form (±3k,±k); do not allow ± sqrt(10k^2-7) or a value found by incorrectly halving thinking it was the diameter). (3 marks)
(b) M1: Substitutes y=2x-1 into the equation of the circle (or their manipulated equation from (a)) and attempts to collect terms, proceeding to x^2+(pk+q)x+rk+s=0 where p,q,r,s are all non-zero (condone arithmetical slips; do not be concerned with the use of <,> or =). A1: correct quadratic 5x^2+(2k-4)x+2k+8(=0). dM1: Attempts to find the discriminant b^2-4ac for their 3TQ and attempts to find at least one critical value for k, i.e. (2k-4)^2-4*5*(2k+8)=0 => k=... (dependent on the first method mark; do not be too concerned with the mechanics of the rearrangement, including values found directly from a calculator). A1: critical values k = 7 ± sqrt(85). ddM1: Attempts to find the outside region for their two critical values, e.g. k<"7-sqrt(85)" or k>"7+sqrt(85)" (dependent on the previous two method marks; must have two values to score). A1: k < 7-sqrt(85) or k > 7+sqrt(85), or any equivalent expression (including set notation) that includes both outside regions using "or"/"∪"/a space or new line between the answers (not "and"/"∩"). (6 marks)

questions.question_text:
The value, V pounds, of a mobile phone, t months after it was bought, is modelled by
V = ab^t
where a and b are constants.
Figure 2 shows the linear relationship between log10 V and t.
The line passes through the points (0, 3) and (10, 2.79) as shown.
Using these points,
(a) find the initial value of the phone, (2)
(b) find a complete equation for V in terms of t, giving the exact value of a and giving the value of b to 3 significant figures. (3)

Exactly 2 years after it was bought, the value of the phone was £320
(c) Use this information to evaluate the reliability of the model. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Sets log10 V = 3 and attempts to find a value for a, or an expression for V when t=0, scoring for sight of 10^3 or the correct answer implied (there may be more complicated routes, e.g. finding the complete equation log10 V = 3 + [(2.79-3)/10]t first, then setting log10 V=3 => V=10^3). A1: V = £1000 cao (including units; do not accept £10^3). (2 marks)
(b) Mark (b) and (c) together - note that work seen in (a) must be used in (b) to score. M1: Either finds the gradient between the two points, e.g. (2.79-3)/(10-0) = -0.021 (do not condone sign slips; may be implied by sight of 10^(-0.021)), or finds the equation log10 V = 3 - "0.021"t (may be unsimplified). M1: Attempts to find the value or an expression for b using their gradient or equation, e.g. scores for the expression 10^("-0.021") oe, or by equating coefficients from log10 V = log10 a + (log10 b)t, or by using 10^2.79 = "1000"b^10 and proceeding to e.g. b=10^("0.61659..."). A1ft: Complete correct equation V = "1000"*(awrt 0.953)^t, following through on their "1000" (just stating the values of a and b is A0ft unless the equation is subsequently written in part (c) before substituting t=24). (3 marks)
(c) Mark (b) and (c) together. M1: A full and valid attempt to either substitute t=24 into their model V=ab^t (where a is positive) and find a value for V, or substitute t=24 into the log form and find V (also finding log10 320 if needed for comparison), or substitute V=320 into their model and find a value for t (do not be too concerned with the mechanics of the solution, but two comparable values must be found - usually 320 and a value for V, or values of t to compare with t=24). A1: Compares their awrt £313-£315 with £320 (or their awrt t=23.5-23.7 with t=24, or log10 320=2.505... with 2.496) and makes a valid conclusion with a reason, requiring: correct calculations (allowing use of percentage error, awrt 1.4%-2.4% for the pound comparison), a reason such as "the values are close/similar/approximately equal", and a statement that it is a "good"/"accurate" model or similar (do not allow incorrect statements such as the model being inaccurate, or comments that only note it as an underestimate without further comment). (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
y = sin x, where x is measured in radians.
Use differentiation from first principles to show that
dy/dx = cos x
You may
• use without proof the formula for sin(A ± B)
• assume that as h -> 0, sin h / h -> 1 and (cos h - 1)/h -> 0
(5)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
Allow the use of h = δx if used consistently throughout; there is no requirement to see the words "gradient of chord" written down.
B1: Gives the correct fraction for the gradient of the chord, e.g. [sin(x+h)-sin x]/h, or an equivalent such as [sin x - sin(x+h)]/(-h) (condone invisible brackets; may be implied by sin x cos h + cos x sin h - sin x, all over h). M1: Uses the compound angle formula for sin(x±h) to give sin x cos h ± cos x sin h. A1: Achieves [sin x cos h + cos x sin h - sin x]/h, or equivalent (may be implied by further work; allow invisible brackets to be recovered). dM1: Dependent on both the B and M marks; a complete attempt to apply the given limits to the gradient of the chord, isolating (cos h - 1)/h and replacing with 0, and isolating (sin h)/h and replacing with 1, e.g. sin x*[(cos h-1)/h] + cos x*[(sin h)/h] = sin x*0 + cos x*1 (condone if limit notation remains present after the limits have been applied; small-angle-approximation routes are also accepted with equivalent milestones). A1*: Uses correct mathematical language of limiting arguments (must see h->0 explicitly at some point, linked to dy/dx) to show dy/dx = cos x with no errors seen (cso); withhold this mark if there is no evidence of limiting arguments (e.g. simply substituting h=0), if a different variable is used inconsistently, or if there was incorrect bracketing when isolating (cos h - 1). (5 marks)

questions.question_text:
On a roller coaster ride, passengers travel in carriages around a track.
• the maximum vertical height of a carriage above the ground is 60 m
• a carriage starts a circuit at a vertical height of 2 m above the ground
• the ground is horizontal

The vertical height, H m, of a carriage above the ground, t seconds after the carriage starts the first circuit, is modelled by the equation
H = a - b(t - 20)^2
where a and b are positive constants.
(a) Find a complete equation for the model. (3)
(b) Use the model to determine the height of the carriage above the ground when t = 40 (1)

On the ride, carriages complete multiple circuits of the track such that in an alternative model, the vertical height, H m, of a carriage above the ground, t seconds after the carriage starts the first circuit, is given by
H = 29 cos(9t + α)° + β, 0 ≤ α < 360°
where α and β are constants.
(c) Find a complete equation for the alternative model. (2)

Given that the carriage moves continuously for 2 minutes,
(d) give a reason why the alternative model would be more appropriate. (1)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: a = 60 (may be seen in the final equation of the model, or implied by 60 substituted for a). M1: Attempts to find b by substituting t=0, H=2 and their a into the model, proceeding to a value for b (may be seen as two simultaneous equations: 2=a-b(-20)^2 and 60=a-b(20-20)^2, proceeding to a value for b). A1: H = 60 - 0.145(t-20)^2, or an exact equivalent such as H = -(29/200)t^2 + 5.8t + 2, isw once a correct model in terms of H and t is seen (stating just a=60, b=0.145 without the full equation scores A0). (3 marks)
(b) B1: Height = 2 m cao (condone lack of units; can be scored even if their model in (a) is incorrect, e.g. by using symmetry of the model to deduce this). (1 mark)
(c) M1: α=180 or β=31 (condone α given as π). A1: H = 29cos(9t+180)°+31, or equivalent, e.g. H = -29cos(9t)°+31, isw once a correct equation in terms of H and t is seen (just stating α=180, β=31 without the full equation scores A0; a correct equation with no working shown scores both marks; the degree symbol is not required). (2 marks)
(d) B1: A reason making reference to any of: the alternative model allows repetition (e.g. "multiple cycles", "repeated circuits", "cyclical", "periodic", "loops around", "the original model can only go up and down once"); the alternative model shows the carriage back at the start after 2 minutes (e.g. "at 2 mins, H=2"); the original/quadratic model would give a negative (impossible) height after 40 seconds or later; the original model after 2 minutes would not be back at the start (vague responses on their own, e.g. "the original model is a parabola", are not sufficient; if calculations are used they must be correct using a correct model, rounded/truncated values allowed). (1 mark)

questions.question_text:
Prove, using algebra, that
(n + 1)^3 - n^3
is odd for all n ∈ ℤ+ (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
General guidance: a mixture of methods/approaches is likely; mark the approach scoring the highest number of marks. There should be no errors in the algebra, but allow e.g. invisible brackets to be "recovered". Withhold the final mark if n is used instead of k, or if the conclusion refers to n∈ℝ (n∈ℤ+ is acceptable).
Main scheme (algebraic method using n=2k and n=2k±1) - you will need to look at both cases (odd and even n) and mark the one which is fully correct first.
M1: For the key step, attempts to find (n+1)^3-n^3 when n=2k or n=2k±1, and attempts to multiply out and simplify to a three-term quadratic (allow equivalent representations of odd/even, e.g. n=2k+2 or 2n±5; condone arithmetical slips and condone the use of e.g. n=2n and n=2n±1). A1: A complete argument for n=2k or n=2k+1 (or n=2k-1) showing the result is odd, requiring: a correct simplified quadratic expression (e.g. 12k^2+6k+1 when n=2k, 12k^2+18k+7 when n=2k+1, 12k^2-6k+1 when n=2k-1; may be factorised), a reason why the expression is odd (e.g. writing it as 2k(6k+3)+1, or via a divisibility argument), and a "hence odd" conclusion for that case. dM1: Attempts to find (n+1)^3-n^3 for both n=2k and n=2k+1 (or n=2k-1) and attempts to multiply out and simplify each to a three-term quadratic (dependent on the previous method mark; condone the same slips as above). A1*: A complete argument for both n=2k and n=2k+1 (or n=2k-1), requiring for both cases: correct simplified expressions (which may be factorised), a reason why each is odd, a minimal conclusion for each (which may be within the overall final conclusion), and an overall concluding statement covering all n, e.g. "Hence odd for all n(∈ℤ+)" (accept "hence proven", "statement proved", "QED") - given answer, so working must be fully shown for both cases. (4 marks)
Alternative valid methods seen include: an algebraic-with-logic method (multiplying out to 3n^2+3n+1, factorising as 3n(n+1)+1, and arguing n(n+1) is always even as the product of two consecutive integers, so 3n(n+1)+1 is odd); a proof-by-contradiction method (setting 3n^2+3n+1=2k for some integer k, rearranging to 3n(n+1)=2k-1, and reaching a contradiction since 3n(n+1) must be even); a pure-logic method considering odd/even n separately with no algebraic manipulation (scores a maximum of SC 1010 if fully correct); and (Further Maths) a proof by induction. Each alternative scores by the same M1A1dM1A1* mark allocation applied to its own equivalent milestones (see full mark scheme notes for exact wording of each).

questions.question_text:
A curve has equation y = f(x), where
f(x) = 7xe^x / sqrt(e^(3x) - 2), x > (1/3)ln 2
(a) Show that
f'(x) = [7e^x(e^(3x)(2 - x) + Ax + B)] / [2(e^(3x) - 2)^(3/2)]
where A and B are constants to be found. (5)
(b) Hence show that the x coordinates of the turning points of the curve are solutions of the equation
x = (2e^(3x) - 4) / (e^(3x) + 4) (2)

The equation x = (2e^(3x) - 4)/(e^(3x) + 4) has two positive roots α and β where β > α
A student uses the iteration formula
x_(n+1) = (2e^(3x_n) - 4) / (e^(3x_n) + 4)
in an attempt to find approximations for α and β
Diagram 1 shows a plot of part of the curve with equation y = (2e^(3x) - 4)/(e^(3x) + 4) and part of the line with equation y = x
Using Diagram 1 on page 42
(c) draw a staircase diagram to show that the iteration formula starting with x1 = 1 can be used to find an approximation for β (1)

Use the iteration formula with x1 = 1, to find, to 3 decimal places,
(d) (i) the value of x2
 (ii) the value of β (3)

Using a suitable interval and a suitable function that should be stated
(e) show that α = 0.432 to 3 decimal places. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts the product rule on 7xe^x (or xe^x), achieving an expression of the form ...xe^x ± ...e^x (if the quotient rule is clearly applied to this factor instead, score M0). A1: k(xe^x+e^x), e.g. 7(xe^x+e^x), or equivalent unsimplified form (may be implied by further work). B1: d/dx[(e^(3x)-2)^(1/2)] = (1/2)*3e^(3x)*(e^(3x)-2)^(-1/2), simplified or unsimplified. dM1: Attempts to use the quotient rule (dependent on the previous method mark), achieving an expression of the form f'(x) = [(e^(3x)-2)^(1/2)("7"xe^x+"7"e^x) - (3/2)e^(3x)(e^(3x)-2)^(-1/2)*"7"xe^x] / (e^(3x)-2) (or the equivalent applying the product rule to xe^x*(e^(3x)-2)^(-1/2) directly; do not condone invisible brackets; the constants for "7" and "3/2" need not be correct at this stage). A1: f'(x) = [7e^x(e^(3x)(2-x)+Ax+B)] / [2(e^(3x)-2)^(3/2)] with A=-4, B=-4, following a fully correct differentiated expression. (5 marks)
(b) Note: if they do not have values A=-4, B=-4 in (a) (which may be seen later), the maximum score in (b) is M1A0*. M1: Sets their e^(3x)(2-x)+Ax+B equal to zero (using their A and B), collects the terms in x on one side of the equation and the non-x terms on the other, and attempts to factorise the x-side with x as a common factor (condone sign slips only for this mark). A1*: Achieves x = (2e^(3x)-4)/(e^(3x)+4) with no errors, including invisible brackets (given answer, so working must be fully shown; if they do not reach the printed answer exactly, this is A0). (2 marks)
(c) B1: Starting at x1=1, draws at least 2 sets of vertical and horizontal lines (dashes allowed, arrows not required) tending to β, finishing at the point of intersection representing the root (condone the initial vertical line not starting from the x-axis; any lines drawn to the left of x=1 score B0). (1 mark)
(d)(i) M1: Substitutes x1=1 into the iterative formula (values embedded in the formula is sufficient; may be implied by awrt 1.50). A1: x2 = awrt 1.502, isw. (ii) dB1: β = 1.968 cao (can only be scored if the M1 in (d)(i) is scored); SC: if x2 is rounded to 1.50, allow β=1.97 to score M1A0dB1 overall for part (d). (3 marks)
(e) M1: Attempts to substitute x=0.4315 and x=0.4325 into a suitable function (e.g. h(x)=x-(2e^(3x)-4)/(e^(3x)+4), or f'(x), or the numerator g(x)=e^(3x)(2-x)-4x-4) and gets at least one value correct, rounded or truncated to 1 significant figure (a tighter interval containing the root is also allowed; if no function is stated this may be implied by their calculated values). A1: Both calculations correct (rounded/truncated to 1sf, e.g. h(0.4315)=-0.000297, h(0.4325)=0.000947), together with a statement that there is a change of sign and that the function used is continuous (must refer to the actual function used for the substitution, which is not f(x) itself), and a minimal conclusion, e.g. "hence α=0.432" ("hence root" alone is not sufficient). (2 marks)
